terms.gloss: itself (as object), referring to the subject
terms.grammar: pronoun, reflexive: genitive suī, dative sibi, accusative and ablative sē; the same for every gender and number
terms.comment: For a thing as for a person: nē sē moveat, so that it doesn’t move (itself); ut sē ērigat, to raise itself. Many English “itself” verbs are plain verbs or passives in Latin (mōrēs sē dētegunt or mōrēs dēteguntur).

terms.gloss: itself (for emphasis: the thing itself, of its own accord)
terms.comment: Agrees in gender with the noun: ipse vacuus locus, the empty place itself; ex ipsā farīnā, from the flour itself; rēs ipsa, the thing itself. “By itself, of its own accord” is ipse or suā sponte (see own).

phrases.latin: sī movēbitur, eximitō; dēnuō eōdem modō facitō, nē sē moveat
phrases.english: If it moves, take it out; do it again the same way, so that it doesn’t move.

phrases.latin: vītis quidem, quae nātūrā cadūca est et, nisi fulta est, fertur ad terram, eadem, ut sē ērigat, claviculīs suīs quasi manibus quicquid est nacta complectitur
phrases.english: The vine, which by nature droops and falls to the ground unless it is propped, raises itself by clasping with its tendrils, as with hands, whatever it finds.

phrases.latin: sī quid forte abest, ipse vacuus locus admonet, ut, quod deest, requīrātur
phrases.english: If anything happens to be missing, the empty place itself reminds you to look for what is lacking.

phrases.latin: nunc fermentum fit ex ipsā farīnā, quae subigitur priusquam addātur sāl, ad pultis modum dēcocta et relicta, dōnec acēscat
phrases.english: Now leaven is made from the flour itself, which is kneaded before salt is added, boiled to a porridge and left until it turns sour.

phrases.latin: dōnec quiētem ipse timor circumspectantibus aquam fēcisset
phrases.english: until fear itself had made them keep still, as they looked round at the water

sources: Lewis & Short: sui · Lewis & Short: ipse
Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cato, loci-cicero-philosophica, loci-livius, loci-plinius), checked against the editions named there.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
